newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lazard exit raises questions on future structure.
newsitem.headline: Lazard exit raises questions on future structure.

text.p: Edouard Stern, once seen as heir apparent to the Lazard Freres investment throne, has resigned, the investment bank said on Friday, leaving open questions about the future leadership of the secretive transatlantic group.

Stern, son-in-law of Michel David-Weill, the hugely wealthy financier who runs the blue chip bank's French and U.S. operations, quit this week as managing partner to direct his own investment fund, a Lazard spokesman told Reuters.

His move was smoothed by a golden handshake in the form of a $300 million investment in the fund from two holdings controlled by Lazard. Another $300 million will be staked by investors led by Stern, one of France's richest men in his own right.
Rumours had been flying for months that Stern, 42, was on his way out of the venerable group, made up of three loosely allied banks in Paris, New York and London.
There had been a raft of reports that his aggressive style had led to clashes with fellow partners and that he had fallen out with his father-in-law.
In January, David-Weill, 64, took the unusual step of going public with denials of reports of a succession crisis at the 150-year-old bank.

David-Weill, whose family has dominated the firm for four generations, said there was no truth to rumours, rife since Stern joined in 1992, that he was being groomed to succeed him and made it clear he had no immediate plans to retire.
Under Lazard's statutes, David-Weill would normally step down at 70 but "there are exceptions allowing partners to stay on longer than age 70," the Lazard spokesman said.

With Stern's departure and the expected appointment of Lazard Freres' top U.S. deal maker, Felix Rohatyn, as U.S. ambassador to France, David-Weill now -- more than ever -- appears to be calling the shots in an ever more competitive investment banking climate, French press reports said.
While Stern's relations with colleagues were strained, his exit, along with another partner, Francois Fournier, had left a void, the daily Le Monde commented.

They were among the few counterweights to the "old guard" at the bank able to shake up Lazard's old-world approach to doing business, the paper said, quoting one junior Lazard employee as calling the firm a "gerontocracy".
While Lazard is still a dominant player in French investment banking, it has come under mounting pressure from foreign and domestic banks.

This year, for the first time, a French study suggested U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs had knocked traditional front-runner Lazard into second place in arranging mergers and acquisitions in France.
But the Lazard spokesman said the bank had no worries about its ability to keep on top of the competition.

"There are few investment banks with teams with our breadth and depth of experience. Those teams span generations, including many young people. It is an investment bank that has its choice of the best young people," he said.
Despite a more aggressive performance by its rivals, the firm racked up record profits in 1996.

In any event, the days when Lazard can be a one-man show may be drawing to a close. David-Weill has suggested the group may have grown so big it cannot be run by one individual but has made it clear he is not planning any fast changes.
"Looking at a timeframe of 10 to 15 years, we need to prepare for a more collegiate management style like some American banks," he said in January.
One possibility was to run Lazard via a directorate of bankers, one in each of its three main centres, he said.
He said he was determined to keep Lazard Partners as a "holy trinity", saying it would be "three and it will be one".
Another unknown is the future of Lazard's relationship with British media group Pearson Plc.

Financial analysts say Pearson may decide to sell its 50 percent stake in Lazard Brothers in London and nine percent holdings in the Paris and New York Lazard Freres operations as they do not fit with its media assets. David-Weill has suggested Lazard could sell its stake in Pearson to buy back the stake.
